how-many-extinguishers-make-a-site-worth.text:
← Fire extinguisher inspection route margin calculator

How many extinguishers make a site worth servicing?

Most route operators judge a small account by the service ticket: the visit took an hour, it billed ninety dollars, it was fine. That reading is right about the day and wrong about the year. Certified fire-extinguisher maintenance under NFPA 10 is an annual visit — you earn that ticket once — while the recordkeeping you carry for that customer's inspection history bills every month. Those two clocks are what decide whether a small site is worth keeping, and a service ticket cannot show them.

Open the free route margin calculator

The six-extinguisher site that loses money

Take a small office with 6 extinguishers, priced the way a typical route prices them: a $9 inspection fee and a $2.50 tag fee per unit, 20% of units needing a recharge, 8% due for hydrostatic testing, 4% replaced outright, 4 minutes on-site per unit, a 24-minute round trip covering 9 miles at $0.67 a mile, your own time valued at $32 an hour, and $8 a month to keep that customer's inspection records.

FigureValue
Visit revenue$165.24
Materials (tags, recharge, hydro, replacement)$43.68
Mileage$6.03
Your labor (0.80 hrs at $32/hr)$25.60
Profit on the visit$89.93
Monthly share of that visit (÷ 12)$7.49
Recordkeeping, every month$8.00
Net monthly profit−$0.51 (−3.67% margin)

The ticket says $89.93 and the year says minus six dollars. Nothing about the visit went wrong — the arithmetic simply never had enough units to carry a fixed monthly cost across twelve months of nothing happening.

Where break-even actually falls

Holding every other figure above constant and moving only the unit count, the line is crossed at 7 extinguishers:

ExtinguishersProfit on the visitNet monthly profit
4$53.68−$3.53
5$71.80−$2.02
6$89.93−$0.51
7$108.06$1.00
8$126.18$2.52
10$162.44$5.54
12$198.69$8.56
18$307.45$17.62

Every one of those visits looks profitable on the day. Four of them lose money over the year. That is the gap this calculator exists to close — and note how flat the monthly column is: each additional extinguisher is worth only about $1.51 a month, so a small site does not climb out gradually. It needs either more units or a lower fixed cost.

Seven is not your number. It is the break-even for the pricing above. Lower your inspection fee, drive farther, or carry a heavier recordkeeping cost and the line moves up; the point is that the line exists and that it is well above the unit count most operators would think twice about.

The drive is a bigger lever than it looks

A small site punishes a long trip, because the trip is a fixed cost divided by very few billable units. The same 6-extinguisher account, moved from a 24-minute, 9-mile round trip to a 40-minute, 22-mile one:

Same site, different tripProfit on the visitNet monthly profit
24 min, 9 miles$89.93−$0.51
40 min, 22 miles$72.69−$1.94

Nothing about the work changed — same units, same fees, same materials. Only the trip did, and it nearly quadrupled the monthly loss. This is the arithmetic behind the old route-operator instinct that a distant small account is worse than no account: it is not superstition, it is a fixed cost with almost nothing to spread across.

What to do with a site below the line

Add units. The most direct fix and often the easiest conversation — a building with six serviced extinguishers frequently has more that nobody has put on the schedule. One more unit turns the example positive.

Cut the per-customer recordkeeping share. This is the cost doing the damage, because it is the only one that bills in months a site with an annual cadence never sees. At $3 a month instead of $8, the same 6-unit site clears $4.49 a month at a 32.64% margin — a bigger swing than adding three extinguishers.

Stop making it a special trip. If the site can be serviced on the way to a larger neighbouring account, its drive time and mileage stop being charged against six units alone.

Re-price, but know the leverage is weak. On six units, an extra dollar per unit on the inspection fee moves the monthly figure by only about fifty cents. Re-pricing works on a big site; on a small one the fixed costs are the story.

And if none of those apply, that is a real answer too. A site that cannot clear its own recordkeeping cost is one you are subsidising — worth knowing before renewal, not after.

Common questions

How many extinguishers does a site need before it is worth servicing?

At typical route pricing — a $9 inspection fee and $2.50 tag fee per unit, one certified visit a year, a 24-minute round trip, and $8 a month in recordkeeping for that customer — break-even lands at 7 extinguishers. A 6-unit site loses about $0.51 a month; a 7-unit site clears about $1.00. The exact number moves with your own fees, drive time, and recordkeeping cost, which is what the calculator is for.

Why does a site that earns $90 on visit day still lose money?

Because NFPA 10 certified maintenance is an annual visit, so that profit is earned once and then spread across twelve months — about $7.49 a month from an $89.93 visit. Recordkeeping for that customer's inspection history bills every month whether you visit or not. At $8 a month, the monthly cost is larger than the monthly share of the visit, and the site is underwater despite a healthy-looking service ticket.

Does a longer drive change which small sites are worth keeping?

Yes, and faster than most operators expect on a small site, because the drive is a fixed cost spread over very few billable units. Moving the same 6-extinguisher site from a 24-minute, 9-mile round trip to a 40-minute, 22-mile one drops visit profit from $89.93 to $72.69 and takes the monthly figure from −$0.51 to −$1.94. The unit count did not change; only the trip did.

What actually fixes an unprofitable small site?

Three levers, in rough order of effect. Add units — a 7th extinguisher turns the example positive on its own. Cut the per-customer recordkeeping share: at $3 a month instead of $8, the same 6-unit site clears $4.49 a month. Or stop making it a special trip, so its drive time is shared with a neighbouring stop rather than charged against six units alone. Raising the inspection fee works too, but on six units each extra dollar per unit moves the monthly figure by only about fifty cents.

Why does the inspection fee alone not tell me whether a site is worth keeping?

Because the inspection fee only covers the guaranteed part of the visit. Why is this priced per year instead of per month like some of your other route calculators?

Because certified fire-extinguisher maintenance is almost always an annual visit under NFPA 10, not a monthly one — the customer's own staff does a monthly visual check. This calculator prices one certified visit, then spreads that visit's profit over the year to get a monthly figure you can compare against sites serviced more than once a year.

vs-ranking-sites-by-extinguisher-count.h.text:
← Fire Extinguisher Inspection Route Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. ranking sites by extinguisher count

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic habit every route operator already has: sorting sites by extinguisher count and treating the biggest counts as the best stops.

First — extinguisher count is not useless

A route list sorted by unit count is real information: it tells you roughly how much a visit will bill on its guaranteed inspection and tag fees, and a site trending toward zero units is a genuine problem worth acting on. Nothing below argues for ignoring that count. What it argues is that count alone cannot answer the next question — which of these sites is actually worth keeping — because count only sets the guaranteed part of the visit, and everything else is set by what the units actually need and how far you have to drive.

The worked example

Both sites below carry the identical 18 extinguishers and the identical $9 inspection / $2.50 tag fees this visit — so an extinguisher-count ranking would place them side by side. What differs is how many units need a recharge, a hydrostatic test, or a replacement, and how far the drive is.

FigureSite A — 25% recharge / 10% hydro / 5% replace, 14-min driveSite B — 5% recharge / 2% hydro / 1% replace, 75-min drive
Extinguishers on the schedule1818 — identical
Inspection + tag revenue$207.00$207.00 — identical
Total visit revenue$567.90$279.18
Recharge / hydro / replacement materials$162.00$38.16
Mileage cost$4.02 (6 mi)$25.46 (38 mi)
Your labor$45.87 (1.43 hrs)$78.40 (2.45 hrs)
Profit on the visit$356.01$137.16
Net monthly profit$21.67 (45.8% margin)$3.43 (14.7% margin)
Effective hourly rate$181.40/hr$16.80/hr
Price your own sites Have a small site instead? →

Every figure above is this calculator's own arithmetic on the two site profiles described, not a claim about any real route or an industry benchmark. Your fees, service mix, and drive times will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to check, not what they should come out to.

The two places an extinguisher-count ranking goes quiet

1. It cannot see the service mix behind the count

A schedule that lists "18 extinguishers" has one column. It cannot show that Site A's units need five times the recharge, hydro-test, and replacement work Site B's do — work that bills at a fee well above its own materials cost, so a heavier mix on the identical unit count is more profit, not more of the same job. Two sites that look identical on a count-sorted list can be running completely different amounts of billable work per visit.

2. It cannot see the drive

Mileage and labor cost scale with the trip to the site, not with how many units are on the schedule once you arrive. Site B's 75-minute, 38-mile round trip costs more than six times Site A's 14-minute, 6-mile one, on the same unit count — a real monthly cost an extinguisher count never states, and most of the gap between Site A's $21.67 profit and Site B's $3.43 on the same 18 units.

When ranking by count is still the right first check

Watching how many extinguishers are on a site's schedule is still the cheapest way to catch a customer shrinking or a building emptying out, and it needs no calculator. The point at which count stops being enough is when you are deciding which sites to keep, drop, or re-route — that decision needs the service mix and the drive behind each stop, which is what this calculator prices per site before rolling the whole route up against a monthly income goal.

Common questions

Is extinguisher count a bad way to judge a site?

Not on its own terms — it tells you roughly how much a visit will bill, which is real information. The problem is using it as a stand-in for profit. Two sites with the identical 18 extinguishers on the schedule can land far apart once the recharge, hydrostatic-test, and replacement mix and the drive to reach the site are counted, and a schedule that only lists unit counts has no way to show that.

How can two sites with the same extinguisher count net such different profit?

Because unit count only sets the guaranteed part of the visit — the inspection and tag fees. Everything else is set by what the units actually need and how far you have to drive, not by the count. On this calculator's own worked example, both sites bill the identical $207.00 in inspection and tag revenue from 18 units. One has a heavier recharge/hydro/replacement mix and a 14-minute drive and nets $21.67 a month at an $181.40 effective hourly rate. The other has almost none of that work and a 75-minute drive and nets $3.43 a month at $16.80 an hour.

Which sites does this catch that an extinguisher-count ranking misses?

The ones a route list ranks in the middle or even near the top by unit count, because it sorts by units on the schedule, not by what those units actually need or how far the drive is. An operator dropping the lowest-count sites to trim a route can pass right over a large-count site that is barely worth the drive, and keep a smaller one that pays better per hour.

Does this replace keeping track of extinguisher counts?

No. Extinguisher count is still the number that sets the guaranteed inspection and tag revenue, and a site trending toward zero units is a real problem this calculator does not need to tell you about. What it adds is the number count cannot produce on its own: whether a site is actually profitable once the service mix and the drive behind it are priced in.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is account-based field-service software for running a route business across scheduling, dispatch, and every technician. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — is this site actually profitable once recharge, hydro-test, and replacement materials come out.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan and headquartered in Glendale, California, used by HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, and reporting across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not manage a customer list, schedule a technician's route, dispatch a crew, or collect a payment, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes a site's extinguisher count, its certified visits per year, the inspection and tag fees and the tag's own cost, the percentage of units needing a recharge, a hydrostatic test, or a replacement on this visit along with each one's fee and materials cost, on-site inspection minutes, round-trip drive time and mileage, your target hourly rate, and a monthly recordkeeping cost, and turns that into real monthly profit for that one site — plus, once you have several sites priced, a roll-up of the whole route's monthly profit against an income goal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
